MUJAHID:v2p759/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p759/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p759/r1.claim: Mujahid says humanity was created in hardship.

MUJAHID:v2p759/r2.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p759/r2.speaker: إبراهيم
MUJAHID:v2p759/r2.claim: Ibrahim says the phrase means standing upright.

MUQATIL:90:1-4/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:90:1-4/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:90:1-4/r3.claim: Created in hardship means humans stand upright on two legs, unlike other creatures that walk on four.

MUQATIL:90:1-4/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:90:1-4/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:90:1-4/r4.claim: The verse concerned al-Harith ibn Amr ibn Nawfal, who asked the Prophet how to expiate a sin; when told to free a slave or feed sixty poor people, he feared his wealth would be depleted and complained to friends.

MAJAZ:v2p299/r1.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p299/r1.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p299/r1.claim: Kab ad means hardship; Labīd's verse uses the word for conflict.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p373#3/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p373#3/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p373#3/r1.claim: Qatada says humans struggle with the affairs of this world and the next.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p373#3/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p373#3/r2.speaker: بعضهم
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p373#3/r2.claim: Another view says the human was created in hardship and in a distinctive form unlike any other creature.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p528#3/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p528#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p528#3/r1.claim: Kabid means hardship, struggle, and enduring the affairs of this world and the next.

TUSTARI:90:4/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:90:4/r1.speaker: author
TUSTARI:90:4/r1.claim: One reading takes being created in hardship to mean being created amid difficulty and distress.

TUSTARI:90:4/r2.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:90:4/r2.speaker: author
TUSTARI:90:4/r2.claim: Sahl also explains al-kabad as uprightness: the human is created upright in the mother’s womb.

TUSTARI:90:4/r3.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:90:4/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TUSTARI:90:4/r3.claim: Mujahid says the child stands upright in the womb like its mother; an angel raises its head when she lies down, or it would drown in blood.

TAB-FULL:v24p408#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p408#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p408#2/r1.claim: This verse is the answer to the preceding oath.

TAB-FULL:v24p408#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p408#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس، الحسن، قتادة، عكرمة، سعيد بن جبير، مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v24p408#2/r2.claim: One interpretation is that human beings were created amid hardship and toil, facing the burdens of worldly life and the hereafter; reports add the strain of teeth emerging.

TAB-FULL:v24p408#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p408#2/r3.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v24p408#2/r3.claim: Al-Hasan says no creature has to endure what the human being endures.

TAB-FULL:v24p410/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p410/r1.speaker: ابن عباس، عكرمة، إبراهيم، عبد الله بن شداد، أبو صالح، الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v24p410/r1.claim: A second interpretation understands the phrase as the human being's upright, balanced stature, standing on two legs unlike other animals.

TAB-FULL:v24p410/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p410/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v24p410/r2.claim: Mujahid also glosses the phrase as being on an uphill ascent.

TAB-FULL:v24p410/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p410/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v24p410/r3.claim: Ibn Zayd proposes that the human being was created in the sky, which he calls al-kabad.

TAB-FULL:v24p410/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p410/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p410/r4.claim: The strongest interpretation is that people were created to struggle through affairs: hardship is the established Arabic meaning of kabad, as Labid's verse illustrates.

TAB-FULL:v24p412/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p412/r1.speaker: لبيد بن ربيعة
TAB-FULL:v24p412/r1.claim: Labid's line uses the word kabad in the sense of hardship or distress, supporting the preferred interpretation.

ZAJJAJ:v5p327#2/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p327#2/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p327#2/r2.claim: The oath’s answer says humans were created amid hardship, struggling in this world and the next.

ZAJJAJ:v5p327#2/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p327#2/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p327#2/r3.claim: Another view takes kabad as being created upright, walking on two legs unlike other creatures.

ZAJJAJ:v5p327#2/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p327#2/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p327#2/r4.claim: A further view describes the fetus’s head as first aligned with its mother’s, then turning downward before birth.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r10.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r10.speaker: رجل من الأنصار
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r10.claim: An unnamed Anṣari explains the phrase as standing upright; Abu Jaʿfar al-Baqir did not object to his answer.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r2.claim: Mujahid glosses human toil as hardship.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says human hardship includes birth, teething, growth, livelihood, and circumcision.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas also glosses the phrase as standing upright in the womb.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r7.speaker: إبراهيم عن عبد الله
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r7.claim: Ibrahim, apparently transmitting from Abdullah, glosses the phrase as standing upright.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r8.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r8.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r8.claim: Al-Hasan says people struggle through the narrow straits of worldly life and the hardships of the afterlife.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r9.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r9.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3433/r9.claim: Al-Hasan also says people endure the affairs of this world and the next.

NAHHAS:v5p227/r11.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p227/r11.speaker: عطاء
NAHHAS:v5p227/r11.claim: He explains kabad as struggling through affairs.

NAHHAS:v5p227/r12.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p227/r12.speaker: الحسن
NAHHAS:v5p227/r12.claim: He says people struggle through good fortune and hardship, and no one bears as much as Adam's children.

NAHHAS:v5p227/r13.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p227/r13.speaker: سعيد بن أبي الحسن
NAHHAS:v5p227/r13.claim: He says human beings struggle through both worldly and afterlife affairs.

NAHHAS:v5p227/r14.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p227/r14.speaker: مجاهد
NAHHAS:v5p227/r14.claim: He describes life's struggle from being a drop and clot onward.

NAHHAS:v5p227/r15.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p227/r15.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p227/r15.claim: All these explanations converge on the plain Arabic sense of laboring through affairs.

NAHHAS:v5p227/r16.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p227/r16.speaker: ذو الأصبع العدواني
NAHHAS:v5p227/r16.claim: His line uses kabad for hardship or struggle.

NAHHAS:v5p229/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p229/r1.speaker: لبيد
NAHHAS:v5p229/r1.claim: His verse also uses kabad for hardship or struggle.

SULAMI:v2p395#2/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p395#2/r1.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v2p395#2/r1.claim: Human life is in darkness and hardship.

SULAMI:v2p395#2/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p395#2/r2.speaker: جعفر
SULAMI:v2p395#2/r2.claim: Human life is in trial and severity.

SULAMI:v2p395#2/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p395#2/r3.speaker: محمد بن علي الترمذي
SULAMI:v2p395#2/r3.claim: Human beings neglect what matters and occupy themselves with what does not.

SULAMI:v2p395#2/r4.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p395#2/r4.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v2p395#2/r4.claim: As long as a person relies on natural traits and trusts his own condition, he remains in darkness and trial; freeing himself from human qualities brings rest.

THALABI:v10p207/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r1.speaker: الحسن عن الوالبي عن ابن عباس
THALABI:v10p207/r1.claim: He explains human existence as enduring the misfortunes of this world and hardships of the next.

THALABI:v10p207/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r10.speaker: مجاهد وإبراهيم وعكرمة وعبد الله بن شداد وعطية والضحاك
THALABI:v10p207/r10.claim: They interpret the verse as describing humans standing upright with straight stature.

THALABI:v10p207/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r11.speaker: مقسم عن ابن عباس
THALABI:v10p207/r11.claim: He reports that other creatures walk on four legs, while humans were created upright on two.

THALABI:v10p207/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r12.speaker: مقاتل
THALABI:v10p207/r12.claim: He says the verse describes strength and was revealed about Asid ibn Kalda, who could hold down a leather mat so no one could remove it intact.

THALABI:v10p207/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r13.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p207/r13.claim: Another explanation makes human struggle the demands of commands and prohibitions, reward and punishment.

THALABI:v10p207/r14.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r14.speaker: ابن زيد
THALABI:v10p207/r14.claim: He interprets the human as Adam in the middle of heaven when God raised him to Paradise.

THALABI:v10p207/r15.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r15.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
THALABI:v10p207/r15.claim: He says a person cannot attain all that he desires or hopes for.

THALABI:v10p207/r16.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r16.speaker: خصيف وابن كيسان
THALABI:v10p207/r16.claim: They connect the verse with hardship and changing stages from embryo to full formation; another explanation says the head turns downward before birth.

THALABI:v10p207/r17.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r17.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p207/r17.claim: Other views call humans boldhearted and thick-livered despite their weak creation and lowly material, in trial and affliction, or in darkness and ignorance.

THALABI:v10p207/r18.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r18.speaker: محمد بن علي الترمذي
THALABI:v10p207/r18.claim: He says the person is heedless of what matters and occupied with what does not.

THALABI:v10p207/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r2.speaker: قتادة
THALABI:v10p207/r2.claim: He says a person is always struggling with matters of both worldly and next life.

THALABI:v10p207/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r3.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
THALABI:v10p207/r3.claim: He interprets it as being in hardship.

THALABI:v10p207/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r4.speaker: الحسن
THALABI:v10p207/r4.claim: He says people struggle to give thanks in ease and to remain patient in adversity.

THALABI:v10p207/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r5.speaker: عطية عن ابن عباس
THALABI:v10p207/r5.claim: He lists hardship from conception, birth, nursing, weaning, livelihood, life, and death.

THALABI:v10p207/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r6.speaker: عمرو بن دينار عن ابن عباس
THALABI:v10p207/r6.claim: He identifies the struggle as the growth of a person's teeth.

THALABI:v10p207/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r7.speaker: يمان
THALABI:v10p207/r7.claim: He says no creature endures what Adam's descendants endure, even though humans are the weakest creatures.

THALABI:v10p207/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r8.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
THALABI:v10p207/r8.claim: A second report from him interprets it as constrained livelihood.

THALABI:v10p207/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p207/r9.speaker: ابن كيسان
THALABI:v10p207/r9.claim: He defines mukābada as bearing a difficult matter and undertaking its hardest part, from the root for hardship, and cites Labid.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r13.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r13.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r13.claim: The oath ends at this verse, whose statement is the answer to the oath.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r14.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r14.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r14.claim: In hardship may mean that humans are born upright from the womb and remain upright after birth, unlike other animals, as a distinction in their honor.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r15.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r15.speaker: ابن شجرة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r15.claim: It may mean being proportioned, as shown by the following mention of eyes, tongue, lips, and the two paths.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r16.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r16.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r16.claim: It may refer to the difficult stages from drop to clot to lump, from the thickening of blood; the word liver also derives from thickened blood.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r17.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r17.speaker: لبيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p274#2/r17.claim: The source begins to cite a line by Labid as evidence for the hardship sense, but the quoted line is absent from this segment.

QUSHAYRI:v3p422/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p422/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p422/r4.claim: Human beings were created amid hardship and endure the trials of this world and the next.

QUSHAYRI:v3p422/r5.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p422/r5.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p422/r5.claim: Another reading traces bodily hardship from the upright fetus through inversion at birth, swaddling, and the difficult road ahead.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس عن مقسم وأبو صالح وإبراهيم والضحاك وعبد الله بن شداد وعكرمة وعطاء عن ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r1.claim: They say the human is created upright on two feet, unlike other creatures that walk on four.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r10.speaker: الكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r10.claim: He also says kabad refers to strength, reporting that the verse concerned Abu al-Ashaddayn of Banu Jumah, who withstood ten men trying to tear a hide from beneath his feet; Muqatil says similarly.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r11.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r11.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r11.claim: The wording kabad is connected to mukābadat al-amr, enduring its severity and difficulty.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r2.speaker: المنذري عن أبي طالب
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r2.claim: He heard Abu Talib define kabad as straightness and uprightness.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس عن الوالبي ومجاهد وسعيد بن جبير والحسن
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r3.claim: They interpret kabad as hardship; Hasan says no creature endures the struggles endured by Adam's descendants.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r4.speaker: سعيد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r4.claim: He describes the struggle as the trials of worldly life and the hardships of the afterlife.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r5.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r5.claim: He says a person struggles through matters of this world and the next and is always in difficulty.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس عن عطاء عن ابن جريج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r6.claim: The hardship spans conception, birth, nursing, weaning, teething, circumcision, livelihood, and death.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r7.speaker: مجاهد عن القاسم بن أبي بزة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r7.claim: He links the hardship to a mother carrying and delivering a child in pain and to a difficult livelihood.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r8.speaker: الكلبي والفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r8.claim: They mention both upright physical formation and the hardship of human life as interpretations of kabad.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p13#2/r9.claim: Kabad means enduring difficulty; human life begins in hardship and remains a demanding trial, so the world is a place of toil and Paradise a place of rest.

WAHIDI-QT:90:4/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:90:4/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:90:4/r1.claim: One reading says humans were created in hardship, enduring the difficulties of this world and the next.

WAHIDI-QT:90:4/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:90:4/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:90:4/r2.claim: Another interpretation takes kabad to mean standing upright and balanced.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:90:1-5/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:90:1-5/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:90:1-5/r4.claim: Human life is hardship in worldly and afterlife affairs; another view reads the phrase as upright in stature.

JISHUMI:v10p7415/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7415/r7.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7415/r7.claim: Kabad means hardship or severity; the word also describes thickened milk and the organ liver, and is a verbal noun for pain in the liver.

JISHUMI:v10p7415/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7415/r8.speaker: لبيد
JISHUMI:v10p7415/r8.claim: His verse uses fī kabad for a situation of hardship and contest.

JISHUMI:v10p7416/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7416/r1.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7416/r1.claim: One occasion report says the verses through the end were revealed about Abū al-Ashaddayn of Banū Jumah, an exceptionally strong man who challenged others to remove leather pinned under his foot.

JISHUMI:v10p7416/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7416/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7416/r5.claim: The verses apply generally; the wording is the basis for interpretation rather than the specific occasion.

JISHUMI:v10p7416/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7416/r7.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7416/r7.claim: A second reading connects the gifts of the senses to the hardship of moral responsibility: God removed the person's excuse by giving him these faculties.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r10.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r10.claim: The passage was revealed about Abu al-Ashaddayn, Asid ibn Kilda, whose strength let him hold leather beneath his feet against all who tried to pull it; he presumed God could not overpower him. Another view names al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r2.claim: Al-Walibi reports Ibn Abbas’s gloss that humanity was created in toil.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r3.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r3.claim: Al-Hasan and Qatada say people struggle through worldly hardship and the trials of the hereafter.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r4.speaker: سعيد بن جبير وابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r4.claim: Sa‘id ibn Jubayr says hardship; Atiyya reports Ibn Abbas’s detail spanning gestation, birth, nursing, weaning, livelihood, life, and death.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r5.speaker: عمرو بن دينار
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r5.claim: Amr ibn Dinar says the hardship is when a child’s teeth grow.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r6.speaker: يمان
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r6.claim: Yaman says no creature endures what Adam’s child endures, despite being the weakest; the root sense of كبد is hardship.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r7.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة وعطية والضحاك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r7.claim: They, with Ibn Abbas via Miqsam, interpret كبد as upright stature, unlike other creatures that walk bent; the root here means straightness.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r8.speaker: ابن كيسان
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p430/r8.claim: Ibn Kaysan says a fetus is upright in its mother’s womb, then turns head-down when God permits birth.

KASHSHAF:90:4/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:90:4/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:90:4/r1.claim: Kabad originally describes a painful, swollen liver, then broadened to every hardship and exertion; mukābadah derives from it.

KASHSHAF:90:4/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:90:4/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:90:4/r2.claim: The verb kabata, meaning to destroy, likewise originates in striking someone's liver.

KASHSHAF:90:4/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:90:4/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:90:4/r3.claim: Al-Kashshaf cites Labid's word kabad to mean the severity of the affair and the difficulty of its crisis.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p483#3/r17.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p483#3/r17.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p483#3/r17.claim: The oath answers to the statement that humanity was created in hardship.

TABRISI:90:1-20#3/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:90:1-20#3/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:90:1-20#3/r10.claim: A further view says humans were created to bear difficult commands, such as ritual washing in cold weather and rising from sleep to pray.

TABRISI:90:1-20#3/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:90:1-20#3/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:90:1-20#3/r7.claim: Human beings endure worldly calamities and the hardships of the afterlife throughout life.

TABRISI:90:1-20#3/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:90:1-20#3/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:90:1-20#3/r8.claim: Another explanation traces hardship through conception, birth, nursing, weaning, livelihood, life, and death, despite humanity's weakness.

TABRISI:90:1-20#3/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:90:1-20#3/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:90:1-20#3/r9.claim: Kabad can mean standing upright, unlike other creatures that fall forward; Mujahid, Abu Salih, and ʿIkrima share this view.

TABRISI:90:1-20/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:90:1-20/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:90:1-20/r4.claim: Kabad means hardship and severity, related to milk thickening and blood becoming like the liver.

TABRISI:90:1-20/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:90:1-20/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:90:1-20/r5.claim: Labd means plentiful, from things accumulating upon one another; the expression means possessing nothing at all.

TABRISI:90:1-20/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:90:1-20/r6.speaker: لبيد
TABRISI:90:1-20/r6.claim: The poem uses kabad for the distress of a conflict, witnessing the hardship sense of the word.

TABRISI:90:1-20/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:90:1-20/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:90:1-20/r7.claim: Najd is elevated ground, named for its height above low-lying Tihama; elevated terrain generally is called najd.

TABRISI:90:1-20/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:90:1-20/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:90:1-20/r8.claim: The Imruʾ al-Qays line uses najd for an elevated route and names the mountain Kabkab.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r2.speaker: الحسن
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r2.claim: Alternatively, it means Abū al-Ashadd al-Jumaḥī.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r3.speaker: مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r3.claim: Alternatively, it means al-Ḥārith ibn ʿĀmir ibn Nawfal, who complained that the faith had cost him his wealth through expiations and expenses.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r5.speaker: الثعلبي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r5.claim: A report cited by al-Thaʿlabī identifies al-insān as al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r6.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وسعيد بن جبير وأبو عبيدة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r6.claim: Kabad can mean strain and hardship; al-Ḥasan says people must struggle with gratitude in ease and patience in hardship, worldly trials, and afterlife trials.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r7.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r7.claim: Kabad means severe effort and grappling with the affairs of this world and the next.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r8.speaker: ابن عباس عن مقسم، عكرمة، الضحاك، عطية، الفراء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r8.claim: Alternatively, humans are created upright, walking on two legs unlike other animals; on this view kabad means straightness and balance.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r9.speaker: ابن زيد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p128/r9.claim: Alternatively, Adam was created in the middle of heaven.

RAZI:90:4/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r1.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
RAZI:90:4/r1.claim: The author of al-Kashshaf derives كبَد from liver pain and swelling, extended to every hardship; مكابدة comes from this root.

RAZI:90:4/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r10.speaker: author
RAZI:90:4/r10.claim: He adds that worldly pleasure is only relief from pain: eating relieves hunger and clothing relieves heat or cold, so a person has pain or temporary escape into another pain.

RAZI:90:4/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r11.speaker: author
RAZI:90:4/r11.claim: This hardship argument entails resurrection: a merciful, wise Creator would not make pain the final purpose; mere nonexistence would suffice if neither pain nor pleasure were intended, while worldly pleasure is absent.

RAZI:90:4/r12.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI:90:4/r12.claim: On the uprightness reading, Ibn Abbas says humans stand erect while other animals walk bent; this form is a favor.

RAZI:90:4/r13.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r13.speaker: الكلبي
RAZI:90:4/r13.claim: On the strength reading, al-Kalbi says the verse was revealed about Abu al-Ashadd of Banu Jumah, who was so strong that leather pulled from under his feet tore while his feet remained steady.

RAZI:90:4/r14.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r14.speaker: author
RAZI:90:4/r14.claim: The author says the first interpretation, hardship, best fits the verse.

RAZI:90:4/r15.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r15.speaker: author
RAZI:90:4/r15.claim: The prepositions في and لام are close in meaning, but في also portrays hardship as a surrounding container, enclosing the person in toil and trial.

RAZI:90:4/r16.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r16.speaker: author
RAZI:90:4/r16.claim: Some restrict الإنسان to the particular strong man just described; most take it generally, while allowing that his action occasioned the revelation.

RAZI:90:4/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r2.speaker: آخرون
RAZI:90:4/r2.claim: Others derive كبَد from severity and thickness, as milk thickens and the liver is thickened blood; on this account the hardship sense precedes the organ name.

RAZI:90:4/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r3.speaker: author
RAZI:90:4/r3.claim: The two etymologies differ over direction: one derives hardship from the organ, the other derives the organ’s name from the sense of hardship and thickness.

RAZI:90:4/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r4.speaker: author
RAZI:90:4/r4.claim: A second lexical view understands كبَد as uprightness and straightness.

RAZI:90:4/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r5.speaker: author
RAZI:90:4/r5.claim: A third lexical view understands it as severity of constitution and physical strength.

RAZI:90:4/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r6.speaker: author
RAZI:90:4/r6.claim: If كبَد means hardship, it may cover worldly hardships: human life passes through pregnancy, nursing, earning a livelihood, and death.

RAZI:90:4/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r7.speaker: الحسن
RAZI:90:4/r7.claim: Al-Hasan applies the hardship to religion: people struggle to give thanks in ease, endure adversity patiently, and bear the trials of worship.

RAZI:90:4/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r8.speaker: author
RAZI:90:4/r8.claim: The afterlife reading includes death, questioning by the angel, the grave’s darkness, resurrection, judgment before God, and arrival in Paradise or Hell.

RAZI:90:4/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:90:4/r9.speaker: author
RAZI:90:4/r9.claim: The author prefers the comprehensive reading that كبَد includes all forms of hardship.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r1.claim: The oath ends here and its answer follows; God may swear by any created thing to honor it.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r10.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r10.claim: He says people struggle with worldly calamities and the hardships of the Hereafter; they also struggle to give thanks in ease and patience in adversity, a view narrated from Ibn Umar.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r11.speaker: يمان
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r11.claim: No creature endures what Adam's descendants endure, even though humans are the weakest creatures.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r12.speaker: علماؤنا
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r12.claim: They catalogue hardship from cutting the umbilical cord through infancy, work, aging, death, questioning, and the grave, concluding that a creator has governed these stages and should be obeyed.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r13.speaker: ابن زيد
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r13.claim: He identifies the human as Adam and interprets kabad as the middle of the sky.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r14.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r14.speaker: الكلبي
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r14.claim: The verse was revealed about Abu al-Ashaddayn of Banu Jumah, who challenged ten men to pull an ʿUkāẓ hide from under his feet; 90:5 alludes to his strength.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r15.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r15.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r15.claim: Kabad can mean physically strong; Abu al-Ashaddayn was among Quraysh's strongest, as was Rukana ibn Hashim.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r16.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r16.speaker: بعض المفسرين
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r16.claim: Others interpret it as bold-hearted and thick-livered despite weak creation and humble substance.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r17.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r17.speaker: ابن عطاء
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r17.claim: He glosses the phrase as being in darkness and ignorance.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r18.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r18.speaker: الترمذي
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r18.claim: He interprets the human as neglecting what matters and occupying himself with what does not.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r2.claim: The human meant is Adam; k abad means hardship and strain in worldly life.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r3.claim: The root conveys severity, as milk thickens and becomes firm, and a person says he endured a difficult matter.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r4.speaker: لبيد
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r4.claim: Labid's poem uses kabad for distress and hardship.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r5.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r5.claim: They gloss the verse as hardship and toil.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r6.claim: He also describes human hardship from pregnancy, birth, nursing, teething, and other life stages.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r7.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r7.claim: He says the human is upright in the mother's womb.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r8.speaker: النخعي ومجاهد وغيرهما
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r8.claim: Kabad can mean uprightness: humans alone among animals are upright in the womb, an honor in their creation.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r9.speaker: ابن كيسان
QURTUBI-FULL:90:4/r9.claim: The fetus's head is upright in the womb, then turns toward the mother's feet when God wills its birth.

BAYDAWI-FULL:90:1-5/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:90:1-5/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:90:1-5/r4.claim: Human life is continual toil and hardship, from the constriction of the womb to death and what follows; this consoles the Prophet for his struggles with Quraysh.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p340#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p340#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p340#2/r1.claim: Human beings endure the hardships and calamities of this world and the next.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p340#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p340#2/r2.speaker: ذو النون
NASAFI-FULL:v4p340#2/r2.claim: Dhū al-Nūn says a person remains bound by divine decree and summoned to obey and refrain.

QASHANI:90:2-4/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:90:2-4/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:90:2-4/r4.claim: Humanity’s hardship may mean struggle against self and desire, or inner illness and corruption: the thick liver signifies a thick veil over the heart and ignorance.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p478/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p478/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p478/r1.claim: Kabad means hardship, extended from pain and swelling of the liver to all toil and difficulty; Labid and Abu al-Asbaʿ give poetic examples.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p480/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p480/r7.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p480/r7.claim: Most take al-insan generically and fi kabad as enduring the innumerable hardships of worldly and afterlife life, ending in relief in Paradise or multiplied hardship in Hell.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p480/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p480/r8.speaker: ابن عباس وعبد الله بن شداد وأبو صالح والضحاك ومجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p480/r8.claim: These authorities explain fi kabad as standing upright rather than lying face down, a blessing granted to humanity.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p480/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p480/r9.speaker: ابن كيسان
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p480/r9.claim: Ibn Kaysan says the human is upright-headed in the womb, then turns head-down when permitted to emerge.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p481/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p481/r1.speaker: ابن عمر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p481/r1.claim: Ibn ʿUmar says the human struggles to give thanks in prosperity and to be patient in adversity.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p481/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p481/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p481/r2.claim: Ibn Zayd says the human is Adam and kabad means the sky; Abu Hayyan calls such alternatives weak and prefers the general hardship sense.

SAMIN-DURR:90:4/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:90:4/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:90:4/r1.claim: ‘Laqad khalaqna’ answers the oath, and kabad means hardship.

SAMIN-DURR:90:4/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:90:4/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:90:4/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhshari derives hardship from a painful, swollen liver and extends it to every kind of toil; mukabada is related, as is kabata (destroy), originally striking someone’s liver.

SAMIN-DURR:90:4/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:90:4/r3.speaker: لبيد
SAMIN-DURR:90:4/r3.claim: Labid’s ‘fi kabad’ means being in a hard and difficult situation, witnessing the hardship sense.

SAMIN-DURR:90:4/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:90:4/r4.speaker: ذو الإصبع
SAMIN-DURR:90:4/r4.claim: Dhu al-Isba‘’s line uses ‘fi kabad’ for severe trouble and difficulty, likewise witnessing the word’s meaning.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r1.speaker: ابن مسعود
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r1.claim: Ibn Masud, Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Mujahid, and others explain the human being was created upright; one report from Ibn Abbas says upright in the womb.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r10.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r10.speaker: ابن زيد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r10.claim: Ibn Zayd says Adam was created in heaven and that is what is called kabad.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r11.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r11.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r11.claim: Ibn Jarir prefers that the verse means enduring life's affairs and their hardships.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r2.claim: Kabad can mean straightness and uprightness, matching descriptions of humans as proportioned and created in the best form.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas, through Ibn Jurayj and Ata, takes the phrase as hardship in the process of creation, including birth and teething.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r4.speaker: مجاهد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r4.claim: Mujahid describes the stages of formation from a drop to a clot and morsel as hardship, then says life and livelihood bring further toil.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r5.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r5.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr glosses the verse as hardship and striving to earn a livelihood.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r6.speaker: عكرمة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r6.claim: Ikrimah says the verse denotes hardship and duration.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r7.speaker: قتادة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r7.claim: Qatadah simply glosses the phrase as hardship.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r8.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r8.speaker: محمد بن علي أبو جعفر الباقر
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r8.claim: Abu Jafar al-Baqir heard an Ansari explain the phrase as a person's standing and balanced posture and did not object.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r9.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r9.speaker: الحسن
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p403/r9.claim: Al-Hasan says people struggle with worldly affairs and matters of the afterlife, including the world's narrow hardships and the next life's severe trials.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r1.claim: Humanity is enclosed by severe hardship; if left to itself it would perish, and these trials prevent it from claiming divine qualities or union with God.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r2.claim: God made humans weak despite granting outward and inward faculties to manifest His complete knowledge and power; reason and experience show they pursue evil and cannot choose good without divine enabling.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r3.claim: The sura’s opening sentence gathers the ideas of all that follows with inimitable concision, while its remaining sentences display miraculous arrangement, structure, linkage, and fit between words and meanings.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r4.claim: As explained in al-Fajr, worldly ease or restriction does not determine whether a person is honored or humiliated.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p427/r5.claim: Human need for movement and rest, then food and drink, and all their consequences keeps people in continual strain.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p428/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p428/r1.speaker: أبو جعفر بن الزبير
BIQAI-FULL:v8p428/r1.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr connects the sura to earlier passages: doomed peoples regret too late, but their fate follows divine decree; hardship tests them and can block those destined for misery from reflection.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p428/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p428/r2.speaker: أبو جعفر بن الزبير
BIQAI-FULL:v8p428/r2.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr links their claim that nobody can overpower them to divine hardening and cites verses on God’s will to guide or leave people heedless.

DURR-FULL:v8p519/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p519/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p519/r3.claim: He identified the secure town as Mecca, the father and offspring as Adam and his descendants, and ‘in hardship’ as uprightness.

DURR-FULL:v8p519/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p519/r4.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p519/r4.claim: He identified the father and offspring as Adam and his children; human life is toil in worldly and afterlife affairs, and labad means much.

DURR-FULL:v8p519/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p519/r5.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v8p519/r5.claim: He identified the father as Adam, offspring as his children, hardship as severity, labad as much, and ‘does he think no one sees’ as no one can overpower him.

DURR-FULL:v8p519/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p519/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p519/r7.claim: He glossed ‘in hardship’ as being in difficulty.

DURR-FULL:v8p519/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p519/r8.speaker: ابن عباس عن عطاء
DURR-FULL:v8p519/r8.claim: He described human life as hardship from birth through teething, livelihood, and circumcision.

DURR-FULL:v8p520/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r1.speaker: ابن عباس عن مقسم
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r1.claim: He said humans were created upright, while all other creatures walk on four legs.

DURR-FULL:v8p520/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r10.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r10.claim: He glossed كبد as hardship and length.

DURR-FULL:v8p520/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r11.speaker: غير مسمى في النص
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r11.claim: An unattributed report says Adam was created in heaven.

DURR-FULL:v8p520/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r2.claim: He said the human is upright in the mother's womb.

DURR-FULL:v8p520/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r3.claim: He described a guardian angel lifting the mother's sleeping or reclining fetus's head to prevent it drowning in blood.

DURR-FULL:v8p520/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r4.claim: Asked about the phrase by Nafiʿ ibn al-Azraq, he glossed it as balance and uprightness, citing Labid's use of كبد for a gathering in an upright posture.

DURR-FULL:v8p520/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r5.speaker: لبيد بن ربيعة
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r5.claim: His verse is cited as Arabic evidence for كبد meaning uprightness or a firm, straight posture.

DURR-FULL:v8p520/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r6.speaker: إبراهيم عن عبد الله
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r6.claim: He glossed the phrase as uprightness.

DURR-FULL:v8p520/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r7.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r7.claim: He said humans endure the narrow hardships of this world and the next; no creature bears comparable burdens.

DURR-FULL:v8p520/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r8.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r8.claim: He said no creature endures the kinds of affairs that humans endure.

DURR-FULL:v8p520/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r9.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v8p520/r9.claim: He described people as enduring the affairs of this world and the afterlife.

BURSEVI:v10p336/r10.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p336/r10.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p336/r10.claim: The preposition fi suggests the person is surrounded by hardship as a vessel is by its contents; humanity undergoes successive pains from birth, circumcision, schooling, marriage, and children.

BURSEVI:v10p336/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p336/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p336/r9.claim: Kabid originally describes an aching, swollen liver, then broadens to all hardship; humans are enveloped in toil from the womb through death and what follows.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r1.claim: Human beings continually endure hardship from the infusion of the spirit through death and beyond; the word spread from pain in the liver to every kind of toil, and the verse's likely sense is hardship.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r2.speaker: لبيد
ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r2.claim: Labid's elegy for his brother uses fi kabad for the severity and difficulty of a situation, supporting the sense of hardship.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r3.speaker: ابن عمر
ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r3.claim: Ibn ʿUmar says people struggle to show gratitude in prosperity and patience in adversity.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r4.speaker: ابن عباس وعبد الله بن شداد وأبو صالح والضحاك ومجاهد
ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r4.claim: These authorities explain that God made humans stand upright rather than crawl face-down; Alusi calls this and the related fetal-position account weak.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r5.speaker: ابن كيسان
ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r5.claim: Ibn Kaysan says the fetus is upright in its mother's womb until birth, when it turns its head toward her feet; Alusi groups this with weak interpretations.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r6.claim: A possible third interpretation makes kabad a severe illness, namely sickness of the heart and inward corruption; the human then means those God knew would never believe, while other readings take all humanity.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r7.speaker: ابن زيد
ALUSI-FULL:v30p135/r7.claim: Ibn Zayd says the human is Adam and kabad is the sky or its middle; Alusi rejects this outright.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r1.speaker: Sâhib-Keşşâf
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r1.claim: Al-Kashshaf derives kabad from liver pain or swelling, then its sense broadens to toil and hardship; mukabada, struggling against hardship, comes from it.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r10.speaker: Râzî
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r10.claim: Afterlife hardship proceeds through death, questioning by angels, the grave, resurrection, and standing before God until one reaches Paradise or Hell.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r11.speaker: Râzî
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r11.claim: Razi adds that worldly pleasures are only relief from pain: food relieves hunger and clothes relieve heat or cold, so life alternates between pain and respite.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r12.speaker: Râzî
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r12.claim: Because a wise Creator would not make pain the ultimate purpose, and nonexistence would equally avoid pleasure and pain, human hardship implies a necessary afterlife of happiness and honor.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r2.claim: Others make severity the basic meaning, citing the thickening or solidifying of milk; this reverses the first account’s derivation from the organ to hardship.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r3.speaker: some exegetes
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r3.claim: Another view takes kabad as uprightness or steadiness, perhaps from the straight liver or the expression “kabad of heaven”; it sees humans standing upright and spiritually capable of ascent.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r4.claim: Elmalılı considers deriving the uprightness sense from the vowelled form kabad a very remote interpretation.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r5.speaker: some exegetes
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r5.claim: A third view reads kabad as the strength of human constitution, with God giving the body strength; this can be included within the hardship sense.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r6.speaker: Keşfü’l-Esrâr
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r6.claim: Kashf al-Asrar offers a physiological analogy of bodily membranes, vessels, and circulation to illustrate how life and formation emerge through stages of condensation.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r7.speaker: Râzî
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r7.claim: On the hardship reading, Razi says the verse can encompass worldly, religious, and afterlife trials, or all of them together; the comprehensive reading is correct.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r8.speaker: Râzî
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r8.claim: Worldly hardship covers each stage from passage through the loins and womb, nursing and puberty, earning a livelihood, and finally death.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r9.speaker: Hasan
ELMALILI:90:3-7#2/r9.claim: Religious hardship means giving thanks in joy, remaining patient in distress, and laboring to fulfill acts of worship.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r1.speaker: İbn Abbas
ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r1.claim: A second interpretation takes kabad as uprightness: unlike animals that move head-down, humans stand erect, which is a blessing in their creation.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r16.speaker: author
ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r16.claim: God’s gifts guide humanity toward its purpose and establish divine knowledge and power to reckon and punish; the contrast between tranquil and unbelieving souls further explains hardship.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r2.speaker: Kelbî
ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r2.claim: Al-Kalbi says the verse was revealed about Abu al-Ashadd of Banu Jumah, whose strength was said to keep him immovable even when leather was pulled from beneath his feet.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r3.claim: Although a particular occasion of revelation is possible, “human” means humanity in general, not a single named person; the hardship interpretation is the intended one.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r4.speaker: Âlûsî
ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r4.claim: Al-Alusi regards all interpretations besides hardship and toil as weak; he reports that al-Hakim authenticated the hardship report from Ibn Abbas and others transmitted it from early authorities.

ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:90:3-7#3/r5.claim: The verse first consoles and encourages the Prophet by stating that hardship is built into human life, then rebukes arrogant opponents who disrespect him; the earlier promise of success is recalled.

ELMALILI:90:3-7/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:3-7/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:90:3-7/r12.claim: The majority’s sense of kabad is that humanity was created amid hardship: life develops through severe trials, by divine care, so people should endure, give thanks, and show mercy to sufferers.

QUTB-ZILAL:90:4/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:90:4/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:90:4/r1.claim: Human life is continual struggle, hardship, effort, and toil, beginning in the womb and continuing through birth, breathing, bodily functions, movement, learning, thought, and every new experience.

QUTB-ZILAL:90:4/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:90:4/r2.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:90:4/r2.claim: People’s toil takes many forms and ends in different directions: some strive for God, faith, and good, while others pursue desire, wealth, power, or Hell.

QUTB-ZILAL:90:4/r3.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:90:4/r3.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:90:4/r3.claim: Worldly struggle is life’s nature, but the worst loser bears it only to reach greater hardship in the next life; the successful person strives toward God and ultimate rest.

QUTB-ZILAL:90:4/r4.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:90:4/r4.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:90:4/r4.claim: Even on earth, noble striving brings inner calm, relief in sacrifice, and a different experience of hardship than toil spent on trivial or base aims.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r1.claim: The surah is called Sūrat La Uqsim in al-Bukhārī's translation, while muṣḥafs and tafsīr books call it Sūrat al-Balad, either quoting its opening or naming Mecca.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r2.speaker: الجمهور
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r2.claim: Most commentators consider the surah Meccan; al-Zamakhsharī and al-Qurṭubī report agreement, while Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmits a minority Medinan view, linked to interpreting the Prophet's being lawful there as permission to fight at the conquest.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r3.speaker: ابن عطية
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r3.claim: He reports a view that the surah is Medinan except for its first four verses.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r4.claim: It is the thirty-fifth surah revealed, after Qāf and before al-Ṭāriq, and has twenty verses.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p345/r5.claim: Its aims include honoring Mecca and the Prophet there and his forebears, then condemning idolatry, denial of resurrection, boastful waste, ingratitude for human faculties and guidance, and failure to spend or embody faith; it warns unbelievers and promises the certain believers good news.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p349/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p349/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p349/r3.claim: The statement that humanity was created in hardship answers the oath and is the surah's main purpose.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p349/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p349/r4.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p349/r4.claim: The prevalent interpretation takes الإنسان generically, with ordinary contextual scope narrowed to the idolaters addressed from verse 5 onward; Qur'anic usage often uses human for disbelievers because Muslims were then few.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p349/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p349/r5.speaker: الكلبي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p349/r5.claim: He identifies the human as Abū al-Ashadd, also called Abū al-Ashaddayn, named as Usayd ibn Kilda al-Jumaḥī, whose strength was demonstrated by resisting ten men pulling him from a hide; he was a fierce enemy of the Prophet.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p349/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p349/r6.speaker: مقاتل
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p349/r6.claim: Muqātil says the verse concerns al-Ḥārith ibn ʿĀmir ibn Nawfal, who claimed to have spent wealth trying to undermine the Prophet; other identifications mentioned are al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, Abū Jahl, and ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Wudd.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r1.claim: The personal identifications reported for the human have no sound transmitted evidence and do not fit the oath or context.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r2.claim: خلق means bringing into existence what did not exist, and can also mean producing a state that strongly changes a thing's nature, as in the cited examples.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r3.claim: Although exegetes offered varied glosses for كبد as toil and hardship, Ibn ʿĀshūr argues that they failed to connect it to the context and oath; treating hardship as an excuse inherent in human creation would weaken the rebuke.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r4.claim: The contextual hardship is the mental distress of idolatry: conflicting beliefs in divine partners, reliance on God in distress, and denial of resurrection despite admitting first creation; verse 4 prepares the proof of resurrection in verse 5.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p350/r5.claim: The passage parallels the preparation in al-Tīn: first creation establishes God's power to recreate people for resurrection and punishment.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p351/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p351/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p351/r1.claim: The mention of hardship embeds a comparison between the first and second creations, both within God's power.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p351/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p351/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p351/r2.claim: The preposition في figuratively expresses enduring attachment to hardship; the intended worldly torment is the disordered anxiety and excuses of disbelief, paralleling another verse about being in torment and error.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p351/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p351/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p351/r3.claim: The hardship accompanies the idolater from the onset of reason and full awareness.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p351/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p351/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p351/r4.claim: A possible rhetorical inversion makes the verse mean that God created hardship within the unbeliever, conveying how completely hardship inhabits him; other interpretations do not fit the context.

TABATABAI:90:4-10/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:90:4-10/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:90:4-10/r1.claim: Kabad means toil and hardship; human life is pervaded by effort, since worldly goods are never obtained in pure pleasure but mixed with distress, struggle, and calamity.

ASAD-NOTES:90:1#n3/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:90:1#n3/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:90:1#n3/r1.claim: Kabad combines pain, distress, hardship, toil, and trial, requiring a compound translation.

BINTSHATI:v1p177/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p177/r1.speaker: أبو زيد
BINTSHATI:v1p177/r1.claim: Abū Zayd, as transmitted by Abū Ḥayyān, identifies al-insān as Adam.

BINTSHATI:v1p177/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p177/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p177/r2.claim: Qur’anic usage makes al-insān a morally responsible human being who speaks, disputes, bears trusts and duties, and is tested by good and evil.

BINTSHATI:v1p177/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p177/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p177/r3.claim: Kabad appears nowhere else in the Qur’an; its lexical path moves from liver pain to hardship and endured suffering.

BINTSHATI:v1p177/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p177/r4.speaker: الزمخشري
BINTSHATI:v1p177/r4.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the verse describes sick hearts and corrupt inner nature, then limits it to those God knew would disbelieve; the author contrasts this with a generic reading.

BINTSHATI:v1p178/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r1.claim: The author allows the hardship interpretations but questions how the preceding oath about the city and generations connects to them.

BINTSHATI:v1p178/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r2.speaker: محمد عبده
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r2.claim: Muhammad ʿAbduh says humanity is made for toil because people are parents and offspring, each bearing the difficulties of growth.

BINTSHATI:v1p178/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r3.speaker: محمد عبده
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r3.claim: Muhammad ʿAbduh presents the Prophet’s mistreatment as part of the human burden borne by every child of humanity.

BINTSHATI:v1p178/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r4.claim: The author notes that Muhammad ʿAbduh extends mā walad to every offspring of humans, animals, and plants, and questions whether their hardships equal the burden of prophethood.

BINTSHATI:v1p178/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r5.speaker: التبيان
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r5.claim: Al-Tibyān says no creature undergoes what Adam’s descendants endure: the afflictions of this world and the hardships of the next.

BINTSHATI:v1p178/r6.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r6.speaker: إبن عباس
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r6.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains kabad as hardship through conception, birth, nursing, growth, livelihood, life, and death.

BINTSHATI:v1p178/r7.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r7.speaker: إبن القيم
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r7.claim: Ibn al-Qayyim traces human struggle from womb and infancy through responsibility, livelihood, death, the grave, judgment, and punishment, with rest in Paradise.

BINTSHATI:v1p178/r8.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r8.speaker: محمد عبده
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r8.claim: Muhammad ʿAbduh reads the hardship as labor in using one’s faculties, eating and drinking, and protecting one’s family.

BINTSHATI:v1p178/r9.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r9.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p178/r9.claim: The author questions these readings’ connection to the oath and rejects equating the burden of prophethood with ordinary growth and development.

BINTSHATI:v1p179/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p179/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p179/r1.claim: Kabad is the innate human capacity to bear moral responsibility and the hard choice between good and evil, fitting Mecca’s mistreatment of the Prophet and the verses that follow.

BINTSHATI:v1p179/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p179/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p179/r2.claim: Using khalaqnā rather than jaʿalnā signals that humans are created by nature for this struggle of responsibility, moral testing, and accountability.

BINTSHATI:v1p186/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p186/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p186/r2.claim: Returning to sound nature reveals the clarity of good and evil, human weakness before the Creator, and accountability for injustices in Mecca.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:1-4:kommentar/r5.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:1-4:kommentar/r5.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:1-4:kommentar/r5.claim: The oath is an early allusion to human conception and birth; unlike later hymnic or polemical passages, verse 3 describes human begetting, then verse 4 attributes creation to God.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:1-4:kommentar/r6.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:1-4:kommentar/r6.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:1-4:kommentar/r6.claim: The shift to God's act in verse 4 shows that the seemingly autonomous process of begetting and gestation remains subject to divine power; the embryo, not Adam, is likely meant.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:1-4:kommentar/r7.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:1-4:kommentar/r7.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:1-4:kommentar/r7.claim: Human toil means moral effort required by created existence, rather than hardship from deprivation or illness; the opening also evokes creation and divine revelation or care.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r2.claim: The metaphor of climbing a steep path links the demanded way of life back to the toil that characterizes human existence in verse 4.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r1.claim: Kabad means distress, hardship, or grief, and fī kabad probably describes being created for a life of toil, as in 84:6.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r2.speaker: Manche Exegeten
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r2.claim: Some exegetes interpret fī kabad as meaning that the human being is upright in stature.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r3.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r3.speaker: andere Exegeten
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r3.claim: Other exegetes take kabad to designate the sky.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r4.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r4.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r4.claim: The alternative glosses are lexically implausible and seem to project imagined anthropological traits into an emphatic verse.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r5.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r5.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r5.claim: The perfect ḫalaqnā should be translated in the present because early Meccan texts do not explicitly attest primordial creation of Adam from earth; human creation more likely means gestation.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r6.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r6.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:4:anmerkung/r6.claim: Early Qur'anic negative descriptions of humans often recall their createdness, which conflicts with their arrogance, ingratitude, and unreliability.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p316/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p316/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p316/r1.claim: Sūrah al-Balad pairs with al-Fajr: both correct the view that ease proves honor and hardship humiliation, teaching gratitude and generosity in ease and patience in hardship; this yields the contented soul of 89:28.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p316/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p316/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p316/r2.claim: The Balad applies this teaching to Quraysh: Makkah was once barren and insecure, then became prosperous and safe after Abraham's prayer for Ishmael and his descendants.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p316/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p316/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p316/r3.claim: Abraham prayed for provision and security for Ishmael's family; the land received both, allowing his descendants to multiply and gain leadership.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p316/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p316/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p316/r4.claim: After receiving these favors, Quraysh forgot their history, treated prosperity as a birthright, and balked at spending in God's way.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p317/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p317/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p317/r1.claim: Quraysh's wealth is spent on amusement and waste; they praise God, persevere, and show kindness rarely, and lack resolve to sacrifice for the needy, thus heading toward Hell.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p317/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p317/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p317/r3.claim: Verses 1–4 cite Makkah's early barren history and the Ishmaelites' hardship, then God's favor, Abraham's prayer, and the House's blessing as causes of security and abundant provision.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p318/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p318/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p318/r2.claim: The oath by Makkah witnesses the claim in 90:4 that humans were created in hardship; like the Qur'anic oath in 95:3, it is evidence rather than an oath based on sacred status.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r1.claim: Kabad means hardship and toil; although the verse can include all humans, Islahi says its immediate addressees are the Ishmaelites, especially Quraysh.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r2.claim: The verse recalls Ishmael’s settlement in a barren, insecure land, where life was nomadic, exposed, and dependent on protecting people and herds.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r3.claim: Abraham’s prayer, the House’s sanctity and custodianship, and safe trade journeys brought abundant sustenance and changed Quraysh’s toil into ease.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r4.claim: Quraysh became vain in their comfort, treating wealth as birthright and claiming freedom to spend without God or the Prophet’s interference.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p320/r5.claim: The Qur’an recalls the House’s history to warn Quraysh that rebellion after divine favors invites their destruction.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r1.claim: Abraham settled Ishmael in barren Makkah to protect him from a polytheistic environment.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r2.claim: Abraham built the House as a worship center for his descendants and prayed that people’s hearts would turn toward it and them.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r3.claim: Because Makkah was barren and unsafe, Abraham also prayed for abundant food and security for its inhabitants.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r4.claim: Quraysh’s present status and riches came from Abraham’s prayer and the House’s blessings, not their planning or tribal entitlement.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r5.claim: The favor is conditional on worship, fulfilling the House’s purpose, and believing the sent Prophet; otherwise Quraysh will lose it.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r6.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p321/r6.claim: Sūrah Quraysh says continued blessings and custodianship require worshipping the House’s Lord.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:1/r10.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:1/r10.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:1/r10.claim: The common phrase “struggle for life” aptly sums up worldly existence and also points to the strength and will that struggle develops.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:1/r11.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:1/r11.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:1/r11.claim: The verse also alludes to the difficult conditions and pressure the Prophet would face from polytheists and the need to prepare for them.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:1/r9.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:1/r9.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:1/r9.claim: Kabad means pain, hardship, and toil, indicating that every person inevitably faces needs, sorrows, and difficulties throughout life.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p243/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p243/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p243/r3.claim: God swears that humanity was created immersed in struggle and hardship.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p245/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p245/r4.speaker: الكشاف
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p245/r4.claim: This reading consoles and steadies the Messenger through his suffering at Meccan hands, and marvels at their enmity.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p245/r5.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p245/r5.speaker: الكشاف
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p245/r5.claim: Alternatively, the oath by the Prophet's city consoles him by affirming that every human faces hardship.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p245/r6.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p245/r6.speaker: روح المعاني
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p245/r6.claim: Al-hill as one whose sanctity is violated both condemns the polytheists and introduces the surah's proof that people undergo hardship.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p247/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p247/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p247/r3.claim: The readings are all intended: the Prophet resides and preaches there, is innocent of their sins, suffers violation and an attempted killing, and will receive special permission to kill or capture at the conquest.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p247/r5.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p247/r5.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p247/r5.claim: The layered meanings of hill link tightly to the oath's answer that humanity was created amid hardship.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p252/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p252/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p252/r1.claim: Birth entails labor and hardship, so the parent-and-child oath connects directly to the claim that humanity lives in toil.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p252/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p252/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p252/r3.claim: The discourse moves from parent and offspring to humanity, singling out the human as the central subject of the surah.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p253/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p253/r4.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p253/r4.claim: Kabad means hardship and difficulty; being in toil covers the many trials of worldly life and the hereafter, from birth until the final abode.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p254/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p254/r1.speaker: غير مسمى
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p254/r1.claim: One explanation says a person continually struggles either to give thanks in ease or to be patient in hardship.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p254/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p254/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p254/r2.claim: The preposition fi depicts a person immersed in hardship as in a container; trials surround him until death, followed by relief in Paradise or endless torment in Hell.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p254/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p254/r3.speaker: لسان العرب
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p254/r3.claim: Kabad can also mean strength, thickness, and solidity, as in a hard central mass, tough ground, or a strong bow.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p254/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p254/r4.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p254/r4.claim: Strength is an implication of hardship: someone created to endure severe trials must also be equipped with the power to bear them.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r1.claim: The oath's answer is that humanity is immersed in hardship, and the whole surah's wording and structure serve this theme.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r2.claim: The Prophet endured severe hardship from his people while preaching; callers should prepare for suffering and patience, as earlier believers were tested.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r3.claim: If hill means resident, the Prophet's abuse in Mecca displays both toil and the strength, patience, and steadiness required to bear it.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r4.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r4.claim: If hill means one whose killing is allowed, the disregard for the Prophet's sanctity is itself a source of hardship.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r5.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r5.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p255/r5.claim: If hill means lawful at the conquest, the defeated disbelievers face hardship while the Muslims prevail, joining both toil and strength in kabad.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r1.claim: If the Prophet is free of his people's practices, struggling against custom and undertaking virtuous but burdensome deeds also requires toil and strength.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r2.claim: The Prophet teaches that Paradise is surrounded by hardships and Hell by desires.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r3.claim: Parenthood and offspring connect to toil through painful birth and the strength, persistence, and labor needed to sustain and raise a child.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r4.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r4.claim: The parent-and-child oath also anticipates the difficult ascent and the hardships of hunger experienced by the orphan and poor person.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p258/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p258/r1.speaker: الرازي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p258/r1.claim: If kabad means physical strength, the strong person may imagine that no one can overpower him.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p258/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p258/r2.speaker: الرازي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p258/r2.claim: If kabad means affliction, the verse makes hardship easier to face by asking whether even a person enjoying power thinks nobody can overcome him.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p258/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p258/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p258/r3.claim: The Creator who made a person strong and supplied his strength can overpower him; human power should not breed the delusion that no one controls him.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p272/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p272/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p272/r3.claim: The enslaved, hungry, orphaned, and destitute are among those who endure the greatest toil; liberating and feeding them enact mercy, while they need patience.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p274/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p274/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p274/r1.claim: The surah's hardships call for patience: choosing either path, climbing the ascent, serving the enslaved, enduring famine, and caring for orphans and the destitute all demand perseverance.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p276/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p276/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p276/r1.claim: Patience comes first because the surah has already described human toil, the difficult ascent, and the two paths; mercy follows the subsequent duties of freeing and feeding.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p283/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p283/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p283/r1.claim: The surah threatens disbelievers rather than explicitly promising believers because its opening theme is human hardship, making the punishment of Hell fit the discourse.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p283/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p283/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p283/r3.claim: The surah uses expressions with multiple possible senses: la uqsim as negation or affirmation, hill as resident, victim, or lawful, offspring broadly, and kabad as toil, strength, or bodily balance.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p284/r6.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p284/r6.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p284/r6.claim: The surah is woven around five threads: human toil, breadth of meaning, collective action, patience, and mercy.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p387/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p387/r4.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p387/r4.claim: The compact word ḥill encompasses residence, violated sanctity, and temporary lawful action; unlike ḥāll, it preserves all meanings and fits the surah's hardship theme.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p395/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p395/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p395/r3.claim: The obstacle and its acts of freeing and feeding entail hardship and require strength, connecting both meanings of kabad—difficulty and fortitude—to the following verses.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p403/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p403/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p403/r1.claim: Debtors, people sought for obligations, enslaved people, orphans, and the poor all endure hardship, linking the obstacle's acts to humanity's creation in kabad.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p408/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p408/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p408/r3.claim: Because al-Balad centers on toil and hardship, it merely identifies believers as the people of the right and does not detail their reward; it does detail disbelievers' fate.

STUDYQURAN:90:4/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:90:4/r1.speaker: al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī
STUDYQURAN:90:4/r1.claim: Al-Ḥasan interprets travail as enduring worldly hardships in life and the severities of the Hereafter.

STUDYQURAN:90:4/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:90:4/r2.speaker: others
STUDYQURAN:90:4/r2.claim: Others relate travail to the hardships of worldly life, from birth through death, and say life is toil and trial.

STUDYQURAN:90:4/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:90:4/r3.speaker: others
STUDYQURAN:90:4/r3.claim: Others understand travail as the trials of death, the grave, and Judgment Day.

STUDYQURAN:90:4/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:90:4/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:90:4/r4.claim: Kabad can mean erect or upright; on this reading the verse refers to humans as the only creatures that walk upright on two legs.
